Q: How do I randomize what rows I import from an SAS file? A:

Update: edited to add a much-more-random approach using a database as an intermediary.

Three methods provided:

  1. Working on the .sas file, randomly sampling the start row and pulling 1000 rows after it, definitely sampling bias going. If the order of the data is important (e.g., rows near each other are more likely from the same region/disease/population), then this is likely not good for you.

  2. Migrating the .sas data into a format that can be sampled without loading all of the data into memory. This does by incrementally loading data in the .sas file and pushing into a database, so it's definitely sequencing through all data but discards during garbage-collection. It should work without overloading your memory.

I'll use sample data from the haven package itself, since it doesn't matter if the real file is 100GB or 131KB (as here).

I'm assuming that you cannot read in the entire file at once. (If you could, then there are numerous easy ways to sample rows from an in-memory dataset.) Also, since I don't have a 100GB file (and do not regularly work with them), I do not know that with skip= and n_max= if the function still reads other than the desired rows into memory; if it does then there may not be an easy way to do what you need.

Option 1: random start, 100 consecutive rows

I believe haven::read_sas does not provide any built-in way to randomly sample rows. As such, I think the best thing we can do is randomize where we start loading data (what row number) and then accept that the 1000 rows will be consecutive.

(I'll demonstrate on a single file, I assume you will be able to adapt to your lapply(files, ...).)

The sample data is just a SAS file of iris data, it has 150 rows and five columns. I'll load 3 rows from random start-rows:

path <- system.file("examples", "iris.sas7bdat", package = "haven")
haven::read_sas(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          5.6         2.9          3.6         1.3 versic 
# 2          6.7         3.1          4.4         1.4 versic 
# 3          5.6         3            4.5         1.5 versic 
haven::read_sas(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          5.5         2.4          3.8         1.1 versic 
# 2          5.5         2.4          3.7         1   versic 
# 3          5.8         2.7          3.9         1.2 versic 
haven::read_sas(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          5.8         2.7          3.9         1.2 versic 
# 2          6           2.7          5.1         1.6 versic 
# 3          5.4         3            4.5         1.5 versic

If you do not know the total number of rows, I think you have two options:

  1. Wrap read_sas() and if it does not return the 1000 rows, then immediately re-sample. If the read operation is slow (due to the size of the file) then you might occasionally "feel" this. Perhaps this:

    read_sas_minrows <- function(path, ..., min_rows = 1, iters = 3) {
  iter <- iters
  while (iter > 0) {
    dat <- haven::read_sas(path, ...)
    if (nrow(dat) >= min_rows) break
    message(sprintf("attempt %d/%d returned %d rows, reattempting",
                    iters-iter+1, iters, nrow(dat)))
    iter <- iter - 1L
  }
  if (iter == 0) stop(sprintf("read_sas_minrows: no call returned at least %d rows", iters))
  dat
}

### unlikely to fail
read_sas_minrows(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3, min_rows = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          6.2         2.9          4.3         1.3 versic 
# 2          5.1         2.5          3           1.1 versic 
# 3          5.7         2.8          4.1         1.3 versic 

### impossible condition n_max < min_rows, just to show it work
read_sas_minrows(path, skip=sample(150,1), n_max=3, min_rows=4)
# attempt 1/3 returned 3 rows, reattempting
# attempt 2/3 returned 3 rows, reattempting
# attempt 3/3 returned 3 rows, reattempting
# Error in read_sas_minrows(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3, min_rows = 4): 
#   read_sas_minrows: no call returned at least 3 rows

  2. Use a simple binary-search to empirically find the number of rows. For instance, something like this might give you a good number (assuming that the act of reading 1 row is not "expensive"):

    known_rows <- 1L   # initial condition, if you have a known min then use that
try_rows <- 1e5    # your best guess
stop_margin <- 10 # if this is > 1, we do not need an "exact number of rows", just ball-park
while (TRUE) {
  message("attempting ", try_rows)
  dat <- haven::read_sas(path, skip=try_rows, n_max=1)
  if (nrow(dat) > 0) {
    a <- try_rows
    try_rows <- try_rows + ceiling((try_rows - known_rows) / 2)
    known_rows <- a
    next
  }
  if ((try_rows - known_rows) <= stop_margin) break
  try_rows <- ceiling(known_rows + (try_rows - known_rows) / 2); try_rows
}
# attempting 1e+05
# attempting 50001
# attempting 25001
# attempting 12501
# attempting 6251
# attempting 3126
# attempting 1564
# attempting 783
# attempting 392
# attempting 197
# attempting 99
# attempting 148
# attempting 173
# attempting 161
# attempting 155
# this is within `stop_margin` of the true number of rows
try_rows
# [1] 155

Option 2: migrate to another format, random sampling

Another approach is to load all of the data into a format that can be queried and sampled lazily. Options:

  1. Parquet files would be nice, but slice_sample() has a known bug rendering it unusable here (arrow#38638 and arrow#45139)

  2. Into a database, whether local (duckdb or sqlite) or more formal (postgres, sqlserver, etc).

Since #1 is unusable atm, I'll demonstrate with #2.

library(duckdb)
duckpath <- tempfile(fileext = ".duckdb") # temp here, you may want a permanent one
duckcon <- dbConnect(duckdb(), dbdir = duckpath)

rows_per_pqfile <- 10L # perhaps 1e6 or 1e7 for you?
cur_row <- 0L
while (nrow(tmpdat <- haven::read_sas(path, skip=cur_row, n_max=rows_per_pqfile)) > 0) {
  if (cur_row < 1) dbCreateTable(duckcon, "sasdata", tmpdat)
  dbAppendTable(duckcon, "sasdata", tmpdat)
  cur_row <- cur_row + rows_per_pqfile
}

set.seed(42)
dbGetQuery(duckcon, "select * from sasdata using sample 5")
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
# 1          4.8         3.1          1.6         0.2  setosa
# 2          5.2         2.7          3.9         1.4  versic
# 3          6.1         3.0          4.6         1.4  versic
# 4          6.7         3.3          5.7         2.1  virgin
# 5          5.9         3.0          5.1         1.8  virgin

The load process will use a bunch of RAM. If you find that it has issues, you might add explicit calls to gc() into the loop, either "every n times" or similar, so that memory can be reclaimed.

This will result in a large .duckdb file. I'm not sure if it will be larger/smaller than the original .sas file.

You can use raw SQL as I did above, or you can use dplyr::slice_sample:

library(dplyr)
tbl(duckcon, "sasdata") |>
  slice_sample(n=5) |>
  collect()
# # A tibble: 5 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          5           3.4          1.6         0.4 setosa 
# 2          5.6         3            4.1         1.3 versic 
# 3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 setosa 
# 4          5.5         2.5          4           1.3 versic 
# 5          6.9         3.1          5.1         2.3 virgin

Q: async and defer loading with document ready A:

If you need things to run in an order, then remove async and defer entirely. Move all your <script> tags to the bottom of your page, inside the <body> tag. Place them in order of execution. They will load one after the other, in order. Async and defer, I would only use in very specific circumstances.

Q: I am getting too many solutions when I need only one A:

Yeah, there's a couple of things wrong with your query. First, you're getting the max order id , which is presumably some autoincrement column. It's like Karl's answer is first, mine is second, SELECT MAX(answerid) FROM this_discussion = 2.... but that doesn't mean I have more answers than he does.

Rnofx5 is also right... you need to tell your table what to join ON, cause right now it's creating a Cartesian Product. If you're not sure what that is, for now accept that it's a horrible, evil, wicked thing to do and then Google it after we're done fixing the query.

So, we have orders and order details. Presumably orders does not contain City, so we need order details

SELECT count(o.OrderID), od.ShipCity FROM orders AS o INNER JOIN [Order Details] AS od ON o.{a varible that both Orders and Order Details have in common} = .{a varible that both Orders and Order Details have in common} GROUP BY od.ShipCity ORDER BY count(o.OrderID) DESC LIMIT 1;

Okay, so we're joining Orders with Order Details. In order to do that, we need to associate every order with something in Order Details. I don't know your schema, but from the sounds of it probably each order has a corresponding record in Order Details. In that case, you join these two tables using their ID. Something like

ON o.OrderID = od.OrderID

Now, we are counting all of the orders associated with a particular city... and we sorting them by our count, in descending order. And then we are keeping only the very first record that's returned (LIMIT 1)

Depending on your SQL implementation, you may need TOP 1 instead of LIMIT 1. You tagged mysqli, so presumably this is MySQL and in that case you'd want LIMIT not TOP. But be aware that that's a syntax variation you may encounter at some point
